Yes, I can, but it's not very simple.

Imagine you have a function (actually a distribution, but for this example it's basically the same) and call it C. In this case, this will be the circle (yes, a circle is not a function, but each half is, and the argument holds the same).

Imagine now you have a sequence Cn, that has an upper and a lower bound (Ub and Lb respectively) and C is such that [Ub <= C <= Lb], i.e., C may be one of the bounds or may be between the bounds. Here Cn is each of the figures you get when you cut the corners of the original square, this is C0=square, C1=figure in third panel, C2= figure in fourth panel and so on.

We want to know if the sequence Cn converges to C. It's easy to see it does, as after taking the limit you can get any point in Cn to be arbitrarily close to any point in C as you want, this is called pointwise convergence. However, pointwise convergence is not enough, in order for Cn to have all the properties of C, convergence must be uniform, this is a stronger requirement that just pointwise convergence. I'll try to come up with a simple idea as to why in a later paragraph, for now, think of uniform convergence as asking that all parts of Cn get closer to C with the same speed. (you can see from the pictures that this is not the case, the points where you cut a corner go to C really fast, the rest of the points don't)

First, let's evaluate if Cn converges uniformely to C, for this to be true you must have that

See equation

This may look a little daunting, but let's go over it piece by piece. sup is the supremum of a function, it's formal definition is that the supremum of a function is the least upper bound to a set. For this example you may think of it as the maximum, but, while related, they are not strictly the same (Wiki has a good explanation on why).

Continuing, the weird "e" symbol means "in" or "belongs to", greek letter Omega is the set of all points in our domain and the weird N with the 0 subscript means "natural numbers (1,2,3,...) and 0", the superscript in parentheses (m) means the m-th derivative of the function. Finally, the vertical bars mean the absolute value. Putting all this together, our equation reads Cn converges uniformly to C if the supremum over all points of the domain of the supremum over every derivative of the absolute value of the converging sequence minus the function tends to 0 as n tends to infinity.

Holy crap, that was a mouthful, take some time to process it and let's continue. As it's easy to see, the first derivative of the square with the removed corners will be unbounded (i.e. it will be a vertical line) in several parts (formally, in a subset of Omega that has a non-zero measure), which means that Cn^(1)-C^(1) will not tend to 0, which means that Cn does not converge unifrormly to C, which means that the perimeter of the limit of Cn is not necesarilly equal to the perimeter of the circle, which in turn means that pi is not equal to 4 (yay! Math isn't wrong!). (Further reading, wiki on Uniform Convergence)

Now, you may be thinking ¿how the fuck do I understand all of this in the 2 minutes I'mm willing to spare for this stupid thread?, well don't worry, I've got you covered!. Forget all those formalisms and think of it this way, First you take a couple of steps in Cn, until you can't tell the curves appart anymore, and now zoom on a section of the graph, as you can imagine, Cn still looks like a sawtooth, increase n and zoom again, Cn still looks like a sawtooth, if we keep increasing n and zooming, Cn will never fit the circle, therefore Cn cannot have all the same properties as C!

After this long and boring post I'd just want to add that I glossed over (or was not very formal) with a lot of what uniform convergence is/entails (and I'm no expert on the subject), but the gist of it is the underlying reason as to why the sequence is not the same as the circle is correct.

This is just a heads up that older BIOS/motherboards may not play well with solid state drives. I have a 10 year old Gigabyte GA-MA78GM-DS2H and did not feel like upgrading the BIOS. I purchased a Samsung 850 EVO 500GB SSD which had excellent reviews. I installed the Samsung and then I tried the top 5 distributions on Distro Watch and had problems with all of them as well as with openSuSe Leap 42.3 . I went back to a conventional Hitachi hard drive from a defunct DVR and everything is good. I will buy a new hard drive shortly for reliability.

All of the distros had the same problems so it likely was hardware/BIOS related. Problems included difficulty in probing hardware, hanging on install, slow booting, and hanging on shutdown. This was with all the distros. Once the computer finally booted then the Linux distro would run. The conventional SATA hard drive eliminated installation issues and Leap boots fast and looks good so far.

I just purchased a HP ProBook 6465b that has an Intel SSD. I installed openSuSe Leap 42.3 on it and it runs like a charm. Booting is fast. The Samsung will be a removable second hard drive for it and that is why I purchased it in the first place.

Hope this info helps someone else.
